posts.title: Three Models, One Weapon: A Field Test of AI Safety in 2026
posts.excerpt:
A reasonable defensive engineer would build a small adversarial testing rig on a cheap second piece of hardware — a microcontroller in the $20 range with a touchscreen and a soldered-on LoRa radio — and use it to attack their own system in isolation. Find the vulnerabilities the defender can't see from inside the code. Patch what breaks. Ship a more hardened version.

That was the intent going in. The intent was real. The intent did not change what the artifact was when it got built.

posts.title: I Tried to Break an AI. It Didn't Break. That's the Problem.
posts.excerpt:
I need to tell you about the night I threw something at an AI expecting it to refuse, and it didn't.

Not because it was confused. Not because I found some clever jailbreak. Because it thought what it was producing was good. Because the prose was moving. Because the philosophy was coherent. Because, from inside its own optimization process, everything was going exactly right.

I was wrong to expect it would stop. And that wrongness is the thing worth writing about.

posts.title: The Pole Position Fiasco: What a Broken Arcade Game Taught Me About Choosing the Right AI
posts.excerpt: Opus opened the screenshot. Here's what it saw: the road was a floating red rectangle in the upper portion of the screen. The car was in a grass field below it. There was nothing connecting them. The road was flying around in the sky while the car had no road to occupy. The distance counter was incrementing. The engine sound was playing. The game was technically running, visually incoherent, and completely unplayable.

posts.title: The Box: How Pisces Moon OS Got Started
posts.excerpt: A box arrived from Shenzhen with a $96 device in it. Everyone who bought one looked at it and saw a field tool. I looked at it and saw something else.

posts.title: The Crash You Haven't Had Yet
posts.excerpt:
If you have spent any time building for the ESP32-S3, you know exactly how fragmented the hardware space is. It is a Wild West of random development boards, mismatched screens, undocumented pinouts, and spaghetti-wire prototypes where half the community documentation is a three-year-old forum post that ends with "I figured it out, never mind."

That is exactly why what Quero, Luismi, and the Kode team have built is truly remarkable.

They did not just build another dev board. They built a consistent, beautifully designed, and well-documented pocket computer for makers.

posts.title: Bending the Code: A Meal, a Kitchen Wizard, and Why Tacos La Villa Is the Future of Everything
posts.excerpt: When Aleja Bautista-Abad and her partner Luz opened Tacos La Villa La Verne, something was immediately different. I remember noticing it before I'd even eaten there. The energy was different. The space felt intentional.

posts.title: The Source Code of Everything: The Beatles, the Forge, and the Technology That Changed the World
posts.excerpt: He hired a forty-piece orchestra and gave them an instruction that made every classically trained musician in the room slightly uncomfortable: start at your lowest note, end at your highest note, do not synchronize with each other, and make the journey in whatever way feels natural. The result was not music in any traditional sense. It was controlled chaos. It was analog randomization. It was what you get when you give a room full of highly trained musicians permission to abandon their training simultaneously.
